analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15% and lets investors erase inflation from taxable gains.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 1991 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it; it died without a vote when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other long-held assets from up to 34% down to 15%, with a 7.5% rate for lower- and middle-income sellers. It also would have adjusted the original purchase price of assets for inflation, so decades of price increases could not be taxed as profit. It sat in the tax-writing committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell stocks, corporate stakes, and business property — overwhelmingly households with large investment portfolios, since capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest Americans. The bill would also have exempted capital gains from certain phase-outs that otherwise trim deductions and exemptions at high incomes [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would have cut the top tax rate on long-term capital gains from 34% to 15% for both individuals and corporations, and to 7.5% for low- and middle-income taxpayers with gains [S2][S3].
It would have indexed the purchase price of stocks and business property to inflation using the gross national product deflator, so only real gains after inflation would be taxed [S2][S3].
It would have reduced the minimum tax on capital gains and indexed the annual $3,000 cap on capital losses for inflation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, since lower rates and inflation adjustments reduce tax collected on investment profits. The lost revenue would have meant larger deficits, higher taxes on other income, or smaller public spending than otherwise.

drawbacks.text: Capital gains are heavily concentrated at the top of the income distribution, so the largest tax savings would go to the wealthiest households rather than to workers whose income is wages taxed at ordinary rates [S2][S3].
Lower rates on investment gains widen the gap between how work and wealth are taxed, encouraging tax strategies to convert ordinary income into capital gains.
The revenue loss would have added to the deficit at a time of large budget shortfalls, a cost borne by all taxpayers through borrowing or foregone public spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a large, permanent tax cut on investment profits aimed at the households and companies that hold those assets. Its benefits for ordinary taxpayers were thin — a 7.5% rate for those rare low- and middle-income sellers and a modest indexation of the capital-loss cap [S2][S3]. The main cost was broad: less federal revenue at a time of budget deficits, which falls on everyone. On balance it was a tax cut for concentrated wealth more than for working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 102nd Congress and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob McEwen introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
Eight Republican representatives cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The bill received no further action in the 102nd Congress — no committee vote and no floor action — and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal treasury kept the revenue it would have lost, and the existing higher capital gains rates stayed in place. Wealthy investors who would have paid the lower rate are worse off only to the extent they were waiting on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury and existing tax rates

for.name: Rep. Bob McEwen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the capital gains rate to 15% and index asset basis for inflation.

for.name: 8 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill in support of the capital gains cut.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by Democrats in the 102nd Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the life of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters — the sponsor and eight cosponsors — were House Republicans; the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without a floor vote [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: A 15% rate plus inflation indexing would have sharply raised after-tax returns on selling startup stakes and businesses, which is why the bill was branded as a venture capital measure. The revenue given up would have been made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.

Corporations and their shareholders would have paid 15% instead of up to 34% on long-term asset sales, with basis indexing further shrinking taxable gains. The benefit scales with the size of the portfolio, favoring the wealthiest households.
Long-held business and investment real estate would have gained inflation-indexed basis, but the bill excluded depreciation-related adjustments and net lease property, limiting the benefit [S3].
